name: Khanate of Kazan
info: A Tatar successor state of the Golden Horde on the Middle Volga, ruled from Kazan over the former lands of Volga Bulgaria until the Tsardom of Russia conquered it in 1552.

facts.founder: Ulugh Muhammad (1437 or 1438) or his son Maxmud (1445); historians disagree
facts.predecessor: Golden Horde; the Kazan Ulus of former Volga Bulgaria
facts.successor: Tsardom of Russia (the Tsardom of Kazan, later the Kazan Governorate)

t: Historians disagree whether the khanate began in 1437 or 1438, when Ulugh Muhammad took power in Kazan, or in 1445, when his son Maxmud began to rule there.
From 1487 to 1521 the khanate was in effect a Muscovite protectorate, and its nobility was split between pro-Moscow and pro-Crimean groups.
Ivan the Terrible's forces stormed Kazan on 2 October 1552 after a siege of more than 40 days, and most of the defenders were killed and the population massacred.
dyk: No document of the khanate survived the Russian conquest, and the records of the early Russian administration of Kazan were destroyed during the Time of Troubles.
ev: Ulugh Muhammad, a former khan of the Golden Horde, takes power in Kazan with the support of the local nobility
Maxmud and his brother Yakub defeat the army of Vasily II of Moscow near Suzdal and capture him
Ivan III of Moscow occupies Kazan and places Möxämmädämin on the throne
The Crimean prince Sahib Giray takes the Kazan throne and leads a campaign against Moscow
Pro-Moscow nobles rise in the Kazan uprising and depose Safa Giray
The Kazan nobility accepts Russian terms, giving up the lands west of the Volga
Russian forces storm Kazan after a siege of more than 40 days
The Mari stop resisting Russian rule in the former khanate

sections.foundation:
The khanate grew out of the former lands of Volga Bulgaria, the Kazan Ulus or Kazan Duchy, which may have regained a degree of independence within the disintegrating Golden Horde by the turn of the 15th century. Its territory comprised the Bulgar-populated duchies of Bolğar, Cükätäw, Kazan and Qaşan, and covered present-day Tatarstan, Mari El, Chuvashia, Mordovia and parts of Udmurtia and Bashkortostan.

Historians disagree about the founding. One view dates it to 1437 or 1438, when Ulugh Muhammad, a former khan of the Golden Horde, took power in Kazan with the support of the local nobility. According to the Great Russian Encyclopedia, most sources support a second view, which dates the khanate from autumn 1445, when his son Maxmud began to rule in Kazan. The History of the Tatars concludes that none of the versions is confirmed by even two independent sources. Under Ulugh Muhammad and Maxmud, Kazan forces raided Muscovy several times.
sections.socioeconomy:
Most of the khanate was forest, with only the south adjoining the steppe. The Volga, Kama and Vyatka were its main rivers and trade routes. The urban population worked in pottery, woodworking, leatherworking, ironworking, arms-making, weaving and jewelry, in towns such as Qazan, Alabuğa, Arça, Bolğar and Cükätaw. The khanate traded with Russia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, exporting furs, leather goods, honey and grain and importing luxury goods, weapons, textiles and spices. It minted no coins and mainly used Russian ones. The Taşayaq fair in Kazan was the main fair of the Volga region.

Slaves were also exported. The khan and the Tatar lords held many prisoners of war as slaves; according to the Chuvash encyclopedia, 100,000 Russian captives were held in the khanate between the 1520s and the 1540s, and when Russian slaves were freed in 1551 about 60,000 people returned home by official figures. Captives, especially women, were sold to harems around the Caspian Sea. The population included Tatars, Chuvash, Mari, Mordvins, Udmurts and Bashkirs, and the tax-paying class, the qara xalıq, comprised state peasants, dependent people and prisoners of war.
sections.military:
The army was made up of levies from the districts and towns, the personal troops of the khan and the nobility, and allied troops. Estimates of its size differ: the Tatar encyclopedia gives 30,000 to 50,000 men, the Chuvash encyclopedia up to 60,000. Firearms were used in field battles and in the defence of fortifications, and Russian sources record the defenders of Kazan firing cannon, handguns and bows from the walls. Tatar Cossack troops defended the khanate from the Nogais, who more often raided the farming Tatars and Chuvash than recognised the khan.

Kazan's wars were chiefly with Moscow. In 1445 Maxmud and Yakub captured Vasily II near Suzdal, who agreed to pay a ransom and an annual tribute. In 1521 Sahib Giray led a successful campaign against Moscow, at the same time as his brother, the Crimean khan Mehmed I Giray, attacked it. From 1545 Moscow organised a series of campaigns against Kazan, and in 1552 the forces of Ivan the Terrible, operating from the fortress of Sviyazhsk, built in 1551, laid the final siege.
sections.governance:
The khan was formally the sole ruler, but real power lay with the diwan, an assembly of the highest religious and secular aristocracy. Major matters of state, including the enthronement and deposition of khans and declarations of war and peace, were decided at assemblies of the nobility (kurultai). The highest nobility came from four ruling clans, Shirin, Barin, Arghin and Qipchaq, joined by the Manghit clan in the 1540s and 1550s. The military service nobility included the uğlans, bäks, ämirs, morzas and Cossacks.

Sunni Islam of the Hanafi school was the state religion. The head of the clergy was the säyet (sayyid), and sheikhs, qadis, mullahs and imams led worship and judged civil cases. The khanate was divided into large districts, the daruğas; the Great Russian Encyclopedia lists five, while other works give four or six or seven. The throne changed hands often: Mikhail Khudyakov counted 15 khans in 118 years, some reigning two or three times, and Şahğäli reigned three times.
sections.impact:
Khudyakov described the khanate as formed from an older Bulgar base, with its population and culture, and a Tatar element that brought the state organisation. Volga Turki (Old Tatar) was the official language of administration and diplomatic correspondence, and Prince Andrey Kurbsky wrote that Mordvin, Chuvash, Mari, Udmurt and Bashkir were spoken there as well.

Literacy among the Tatars was fairly widespread, because every village with a mosque also had a school. A large madrasa and library stood at the cathedral mosque in Kazan, and Kazan became a centre of science and theology. Old Tatar poets and writers included Möxämmädyar, whom the History of the Tatars calls the great poet of the khanate, and Qolşärif. The ruined city of Bolghar became a religious and educational centre and a place of pilgrimage. White-stone architecture and stone carving reached a high level. The khanate's trade made Kazan's fair the main fair of the Volga region until, in 1525, Safa Giray agreed at Russian insistence to move it to Nizhny Novgorod.
sections.decline:
Conflict between pro-Moscow and pro-Crimean nobles marked the last decade. Safa Giray, deposed in 1546, returned with Nogai troops and overthrew Şahğäli; after his death in 1549 his two-year-old son Ütämeşgäräy reigned under the regent Söyembikä. In 1551 the nobility accepted Russian terms, but an uprising led by the sayyid Qolşärif expelled the Russian garrison in 1552, and Yadegar Mokhammad became khan.

In 1552 the forces of Ivan the Terrible besieged Kazan. After more than 40 days the Russians blew up the walls and stormed the city on 2 October 1552 (Old Style); most defenders were killed and the population was massacred. The administration of the khanate was wiped out, Tatars were resettled away from rivers, roads and Kazan, and Orthodox clergy such as Germogen forcibly baptised many Tatars. The Mari resisted until May 1557. The Prikaz of the Kazan Palace undertook the forced Russification and Christianization of the Tatars and other peoples, and the term Tsardom of Kazan was used until 1708.

summary: The Khanate of Kazan was a multiethnic Tatar state on the Middle Volga, heir to the Golden Horde and to Volga Bulgaria. Its khans were weak against a powerful nobility and torn between Moscow and Crimea, and its towns lived by crafts, trade and the slave trade until Ivan the Terrible conquered Kazan in 1552.
references: Viacheslav Shpakovsky and David Nicolle, Armies of the Volga Bulgars & Khanate of Kazan: 9th–16th Centuries (Osprey Publishing, 2013)
Azade-Ayşe Rorlich, The Volga Tatars: A Profile in National Resilience (Hoover Institution Press, 1986)

pointDescs.1438: Ulugh Muhammad takes power in Kazan with the support of the local nobility, by one dating of the khanate's founding.
pointDescs.1445: Maxmud and Yakub defeat Vasily II near Suzdal and capture him; Moscow agrees to a ransom and an annual tribute.
pointDescs.1487: Ivan III occupies Kazan and installs Möxämmädämin, making the khanate in effect a Muscovite protectorate.
pointDescs.1502: Möxämmädämin returns to the throne after the brief reign of the Siberian Genghisid Mamuk.
pointDescs.1505: Möxämmädämin breaks with Moscow, arresting the Russian envoy and imprisoning Russian merchants.
pointDescs.1521: Sahib Giray takes the throne with Crimean support and leads a successful campaign against Moscow.
pointDescs.1525: At Russian insistence Safa Giray agrees to move the trade fair from Kazan to Nizhny Novgorod.
pointDescs.1546: Pro-Moscow nobles depose Safa Giray in the Kazan uprising; he later returns with Nogai troops.
pointDescs.1549: Safa Giray dies and his two-year-old son Ütämeşgäräy becomes khan under the regent Söyembikä.
pointDescs.1551: The nobility accepts Russian terms, giving up the lands west of the Volga and taking Şahğäli back as khan.
pointDescs.1552: Russian forces storm Kazan after a siege of more than 40 days and the khanate is conquered.

notes: Founding date disputed (1437/1438 or 1445); the register's 1438 used. Article gives 'several thousand' population decline, left out as vague. Slave trade figures are the Chuvash encyclopedia's and attributed.
